questions.stem: An analyst receives a lavish gift from a client who is pleased with the prior year's portfolio performance. Under the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct, what is the analyst's correct course of action?

options.text: Disclose the gift to her employer
Refuse the gift outright because all client gifts are prohibited
Accept the gift privately since it came from a client, not a prospect
Return the gift only if it exceeds a fixed monetary threshold set by CFA Institute

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity permits gifts from clients for past performance but requires disclosure to the employer so it can assess any conflict and apply its gift policy. Why the others are wrong: **B** gifts from existing clients are not categorically prohibited—only those that could compromise independence; **C** accepting privately defeats the disclosure requirement and risks a conflict; **D** CFA Institute sets no universal dollar threshold, so the test is disclosure and judgment, not a fixed number.

questions.stem: While having lunch with a friend who is a senior executive, an analyst overhears non-public details of an imminent merger. Under the Standards, what must the analyst do?

options.text: Refrain from trading or causing others to trade on the information until it is public
Trade immediately for clients because the information was obtained accidentally
Share the information only with the firm's other portfolio managers
Trade for personal accounts but not for client accounts

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits acting or causing others to act on material nonpublic information regardless of how it was obtained. Why the others are wrong: **B** trading on MNPI is prohibited even if overheard accidentally; **C** disseminating MNPI internally still constitutes causing others to trade; **D** the prohibition covers personal accounts just as fully as client accounts.

questions.stem: A CFA charterholder leaves her firm to join a competitor. Before resigning, which action would MOST likely violate Standard IV(A) Loyalty to her current employer?

options.text: Copying the firm's proprietary client list to solicit those clients after she leaves
Making arrangements to start the new job after her employment ends
Using her general skills and knowledge at the new employer
Recalling client names from memory after departure where not prohibited by agreement

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Standard IV(A) Loyalty bars taking the employer's property—including confidential client records—to benefit a competitor while still employed. Why the others are wrong: **B** preparing to compete after employment ends is permitted if it does not breach duties; **C** general skills and experience belong to the employee; **D** using client names recalled from memory is generally allowed absent a non-compete or confidentiality agreement.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager allocates shares of an oversubscribed IPO. To comply with Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, how should the shares be allocated among suitable clients?

options.text: On a pro rata basis among all suitable client accounts for whom the IPO is appropriate
First to the clients who generate the highest fees for the firm
First to the manager's family accounts, then to other clients
Only to the clients who specifically requested the IPO by phone first

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Standard III(B) Fair Dealing requires that clients be treated fairly; for oversubscribed issues, a pro rata allocation across suitable accounts is the standard fair method. Why the others are wrong: **B** favoring high-fee clients discriminates against others; **C** favoring family or beneficial-ownership accounts violates fair dealing and priority of transactions; **D** rewarding only those who called first is not an equitable allocation.

questions.stem: An analyst bases a buy recommendation primarily on a third-party research report. Under Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis, what is required before relying on that report?

options.text: Make reasonable efforts to verify that the third party's research is sound
Independently re-derive every number in the report from primary sources
Rely on it without question because it came from an external provider
Disclose only that an external report was used, with no assessment of its quality

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis lets members use third-party research only after taking reasonable steps to determine that it is sound (e.g., reviewing the provider's reputation, methodology, and assumptions). Why the others are wrong: **B** full re-derivation is not required—reasonable verification is; **C** blind reliance fails the diligence standard; **D** disclosure alone does not substitute for assessing whether the basis is reasonable.

questions.stem: When may a CFA charterholder describe the meaning of the CFA designation in marketing materials?

options.text: By factually stating it is earned by passing three exams and meeting work-experience requirements, without implying superior performance
By stating that holding the charter guarantees superior investment results
By using 'CFA' as a noun, such as 'she is a CFA'
By claiming partial completion entitles one to use the marks after passing Level I

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Standard VII(B) permits factual references to the program's rigor and requirements but prohibits any claim of superior performance from holding the charter. Why the others are wrong: **B** implying guaranteed superior results is expressly prohibited; **C** 'CFA' must be used as an adjective (a 'CFA charterholder'), never as a noun; **D** candidates may state they have passed a level but may not use the marks until the charter is awarded.

questions.stem: Which two statements about the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS) are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: GIPS compliance is voluntary and applies to investment management firms, not individuals
A firm must apply GIPS on a composite basis, grouping portfolios by strategy or mandate
GIPS compliance can be claimed for a single product line while excluding others within the firm
GIPS is a legal regulation enforced by securities regulators worldwide

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** GIPS is a voluntary set of ethical principles adopted firm-wide by investment management firms, and performance must be presented using composites that aggregate portfolios with similar strategies. Why the others are wrong: **C** compliance must be firm-wide—a firm cannot claim partial compliance for selected products; **D** GIPS is a voluntary standard, not a government regulation, though regulators may reference it.

questions.stem: A research analyst is preparing a report. Which two practices are required to comply with Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients? (Select two.)

options.text: Distinguish clearly between fact and opinion in the report
Disclose the basic format and general principles of the investment process
Guarantee the projected returns shown in the report
Omit significant limitations of the analysis to keep the report concise

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Standard V(B) requires members to separate fact from opinion and to disclose the process and its general principles so clients can evaluate the recommendation. Why the others are wrong: **C** guaranteeing returns misrepresents uncertain outcomes and violates the standard; **D** material limitations and risks must be disclosed, not omitted.

questions.stem: An investor deposits $1,000 today in an account earning 6% compounded annually. What is the account's value at the end of 3 years?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** FV = PV(1 + r)^n = 1,000(1.06)^3 = 1,000 x 1.191016 = $1,191.02. Why the others are wrong: **B** $1,180 applies simple interest (1,000 x 1.18) instead of compounding; **C** $1,060 is only one year of growth; **D** $1,160 uses 16% or a miscalculation rather than (1.06)^3.

questions.stem: A stock returns +50% in year 1 and -50% in year 2. Which statement about its arithmetic and geometric mean annual returns is correct?

options.text: The arithmetic mean is 0% and the geometric mean is about -13.4%
The arithmetic and geometric means are both 0%
The geometric mean exceeds the arithmetic mean
The arithmetic mean is -13.4% and the geometric mean is 0%

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Arithmetic mean = (50% + -50%)/2 = 0%. Geometric mean = [(1.5)(0.5)]^(1/2) - 1 = (0.75)^0.5 - 1 = 0.866 - 1 = -13.4%. Why the others are wrong: **B** the geometric mean is not 0% because compounding a gain then an equal loss leaves less than the start; **C** the geometric mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean when returns vary; **D** it reverses which mean equals 0%.

questions.stem: A distribution of returns has a long left tail, with the mean pulled below the median. This distribution is BEST described as exhibiting:

options.text: Negative (left) skewness
Positive (right) skewness
Excess positive kurtosis only
Zero skewness, like a normal distribution

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A long left tail with the mean below the median indicates negative (left) skewness, where extreme losses dominate the tail. Why the others are wrong: **B** positive skew has a long right tail with the mean above the median; **C** kurtosis describes tail thickness/peakedness, not the direction of the tail; **D** a normal distribution is symmetric with zero skewness, which the long left tail contradicts.

questions.stem: Place the steps of a standard hypothesis test in their correct sequence.

options.text: State the null and alternative hypotheses
Identify the appropriate test statistic and its distribution
Specify the level of significance and the decision (rejection) rule
Compute the test statistic and make the statistical decision

questions.explanation: The correct sequence is A, B, C, D. You first state the null (H0) and alternative (Ha) hypotheses so you know what is being tested. Next you identify the appropriate test statistic (e.g., t, z, chi-square) and its distribution given the data and assumptions. You then specify the significance level (alpha) and the decision rule, which fixes the critical value(s) before seeing results to avoid bias. Finally you compute the test statistic from the sample and compare it to the rule to reject or fail to reject H0. Setting the rule before computing the statistic is essential to a valid, unbiased test.

questions.stem: In a perfectly competitive market in long-run equilibrium, what is the relationship between price and a firm's marginal cost?

options.text: Price equals marginal cost
Price exceeds marginal cost because of market power
Price is below marginal cost to deter entry
Price is set by the firm independently of marginal cost

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under perfect competition firms are price takers; they maximize profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and because price equals marginal revenue, price equals marginal cost. Why the others are wrong: **B** P > MC reflects monopoly or imperfect competition with pricing power; **C** pricing below MC is unsustainable and not an equilibrium; **D** competitive firms cannot set price—it is determined by the market.

questions.stem: A central bank raises its policy interest rate and conducts open-market sales of securities. These actions are BEST described as:

options.text: Contractionary monetary policy
Expansionary monetary policy
Contractionary fiscal policy
Expansionary fiscal policy

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Raising the policy rate and selling securities both drain reserves and reduce the money supply, which is contractionary monetary policy aimed at slowing the economy or curbing inflation. Why the others are wrong: **B** expansionary policy would cut rates and buy securities; **C** and **D** describe fiscal policy (government spending and taxation), not central-bank actions on rates and open-market operations.

questions.stem: The spot exchange rate is 1.25 USD/EUR. If the euro then appreciates against the dollar, which of the following is MOST consistent with that appreciation?

options.text: The rate moves to 1.30 USD/EUR
The rate moves to 1.20 USD/EUR
It now takes fewer dollars to buy one euro
The dollar buys more euros than before

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** With the price currency (USD) quoted per unit of base currency (EUR), euro appreciation means each euro buys more dollars, so the rate rises from 1.25 to 1.30 USD/EUR. Why the others are wrong: **B** a fall to 1.20 means the euro depreciated; **C** needing fewer dollars per euro is euro depreciation; **D** the dollar buying more euros means the dollar appreciated, not the euro.

questions.stem: Which phase of the business cycle is typically characterized by falling real GDP, rising unemployment, and declining inflationary pressure?

options.text: Contraction (recession)
Expansion
Peak
Early recovery with accelerating growth

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A contraction features declining real output, rising unemployment, and easing inflation as demand weakens. Why the others are wrong: **B** expansion shows rising GDP and falling unemployment; **C** a peak is the turning point of highest activity, not falling output; **D** early recovery has accelerating, not falling, GDP.

questions.stem: Which financial statement reports a company's assets, liabilities, and owners' equity at a specific point in time?

options.text: The balance sheet (statement of financial position)
The income statement
The statement of cash flows
The statement of comprehensive income

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The balance sheet presents assets, liabilities, and equity at a single point in time and embodies the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Why the others are wrong: **B** the income statement covers performance over a period; **C** the cash flow statement reports cash movements over a period; **D** comprehensive income reports period gains/losses, not a point-in-time position.

questions.stem: During a period of rising prices, a company using FIFO rather than weighted-average cost for inventory will MOST likely report:

options.text: Lower cost of goods sold and higher ending inventory
Higher cost of goods sold and lower ending inventory
Lower cost of goods sold and lower ending inventory
Higher cost of goods sold and higher ending inventory

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under FIFO in rising prices, the oldest (cheaper) costs flow to COGS, so COGS is lower while the most recent (higher) costs remain in ending inventory, making inventory higher. Why the others are wrong: **B** describes LIFO in rising prices; **C** and **D** pair the COGS and inventory effects inconsistently—FIFO lowers COGS and raises inventory together.

questions.stem: Under US GAAP, a company classifies interest paid in which section of the statement of cash flows?

options.text: Operating activities
Financing activities
Investing activities
It may freely choose operating or investing

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under US GAAP, interest paid is reported within operating activities. Why the others are wrong: **B** financing is where principal repayments and dividends paid go, not interest paid under US GAAP; **C** investing covers purchases/sales of long-term assets; **D** US GAAP fixes the classification of interest paid as operating—IFRS, by contrast, allows operating or financing.

questions.stem: A firm has current assets of $600, inventory of $200, and current liabilities of $250. What is its quick (acid-test) ratio?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Quick ratio = (current assets - inventory) / current liabilities = (600 - 200) / 250 = 400/250 = 1.6. Why the others are wrong: **B** 2.4 is the current ratio (600/250), which improperly includes inventory; **C** 0.8 divides inventory alone by current liabilities; **D** 3.2 doubles or otherwise miscomputes the numerator.

questions.stem: An analyst decomposes ROE using the three-part DuPont model. Which two components, together with the net profit margin, complete the decomposition? (Select two.)

options.text: Total asset turnover
Financial leverage (assets/equity)
The current ratio
The dividend payout ratio

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The three-part DuPont model is ROE = net profit margin x total asset turnover x financial leverage, so asset turnover and the equity multiplier complete it. Why the others are wrong: **C** the current ratio is a liquidity measure, not a DuPont factor; **D** the payout ratio relates to dividends and the sustainable growth rate, not the ROE decomposition.

questions.stem: Under the shareholder theory of corporate governance, the primary corporate objective is BEST described as:

options.text: Maximizing shareholder wealth over the long term
Maximizing reported accounting net income in the current year
Maximizing total revenue regardless of cost
Minimizing the firm's tax expense above all else

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Finance theory holds that managers should maximize shareholder wealth, reflected in long-run share value, which incorporates risk and the time value of cash flows. Why the others are wrong: **B** accounting income can be managed and ignores risk and timing; **C** maximizing revenue ignores profitability and cost; **D** minimizing taxes is one input to value, not the overarching objective.

questions.stem: A company evaluates an independent project with a positive net present value (NPV). Based solely on the NPV rule, the firm should:

options.text: Accept the project because it is expected to add value
Reject the project because positive NPV implies excessive risk
Accept it only if its IRR is below the required rate of return
Be indifferent because NPV ignores the time value of money

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A positive NPV means the present value of expected cash inflows exceeds the cost, so the project adds value and should be accepted. Why the others are wrong: **B** positive NPV signals value creation, not excessive risk; **C** an acceptable project has IRR above (not below) the required return; **D** NPV explicitly discounts cash flows, so it does account for the time value of money.

questions.stem: A firm's before-tax cost of debt is 8% and its marginal tax rate is 25%. What is the after-tax cost of debt used in the weighted average cost of capital?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Because interest is tax deductible, after-tax cost of debt = rd(1 - t) = 8%(1 - 0.25) = 8% x 0.75 = 6.0%. Why the others are wrong: **B** 8% ignores the tax shield; **C** 2% subtracts the tax rate from the cost rather than multiplying by (1 - t); **D** 10% adds rather than reduces for taxes.

questions.stem: Place the typical steps of the corporate capital allocation (capital budgeting) process in their correct order.

options.text: Generate investment ideas and project proposals
Analyze each proposal by forecasting incremental cash flows
Plan the capital budget and select projects that fit firm priorities and constraints
Monitor performance and conduct a post-audit of the decisions

questions.explanation: The correct order is A, B, C, D. The process begins by generating investment ideas and proposals, since no analysis can occur without candidate projects. Each proposal is then analyzed by forecasting its incremental after-tax cash flows and computing measures such as NPV and IRR. Next, the firm plans the overall capital budget and selects the projects that best fit strategy, profitability, and resource constraints. Finally, after implementation the firm monitors results and performs a post-audit, comparing actual outcomes with forecasts to improve future analysis. Evaluation must precede selection, and the post-audit logically comes last.

questions.stem: An investor sells shares she does not own, borrowing them to deliver, in anticipation of a price decline. This transaction is BEST described as a:

options.text: Short sale
Margin purchase
Limit buy order
Covered call

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A short sale involves borrowing and selling a security in the hope of buying it back later at a lower price, profiting from a decline. Why the others are wrong: **B** a margin purchase is a leveraged long position betting on a rise; **C** a limit buy order sets a maximum purchase price and is not a short; **D** a covered call is an options strategy on shares already owned.

questions.stem: Under the semi-strong form of market efficiency, which statement is MOST accurate?

options.text: Security prices fully reflect all publicly available information, so fundamental analysis of public data cannot consistently earn abnormal returns
Security prices reflect only past price and volume data
Even private (insider) information is fully reflected in prices
Technical analysis reliably produces abnormal returns

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Semi-strong efficiency holds that prices reflect all public information, so neither technical nor fundamental analysis of public data yields consistent abnormal returns. Why the others are wrong: **B** reflecting only past price/volume describes the weak form; **C** prices reflecting private information describes the strong form; **D** if technical analysis worked reliably, even weak-form efficiency would be violated.

questions.stem: A stock just paid a dividend of $2.00 (D0). Dividends are expected to grow at a constant 4% forever, and the required return is 9%. Using the Gordon growth model, the intrinsic value per share is closest to:
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Gordon growth model uses next year's dividend: V0 = D1/(r - g) = D0(1 + g)/(r - g) = 2.00(1.04)/(0.09 - 0.04) = 2.08/0.05 = $41.60. Why the others are wrong: **B** $40.00 incorrectly uses D0 instead of D1; **C** $22.20 misapplies the denominator (e.g., uses r + g); **D** $52.00 omits the growth factor or uses a wrong spread.

questions.stem: A market-capitalization-weighted equity index gives the greatest influence to:

options.text: Constituents with the largest market values
Constituents with the highest share prices
Each constituent equally regardless of size
Constituents with the lowest share prices

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** In a market-cap-weighted index, each security's weight is proportional to its market value, so the largest companies have the greatest impact. Why the others are wrong: **B** weighting by share price describes a price-weighted index (e.g., the DJIA); **C** equal influence describes an equal-weighted index; **D** low-price constituents are not specially weighted in any standard scheme.

questions.stem: Which two features distinguish preferred stock from common stock? (Select two.)

options.text: Preferred dividends generally have priority over common dividends
Preferred shareholders typically have a higher claim on assets in liquidation than common shareholders
Preferred stock always carries full voting rights, unlike common stock
Preferred stock has unlimited upside in earnings growth, unlike common stock

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Preferred stock ranks ahead of common for both dividends and, in liquidation, claims on assets. Why the others are wrong: **C** preferred shares usually carry limited or no voting rights, the opposite of the claim; **D** preferred dividends are typically fixed, so it is common stock that has the open-ended upside.

questions.stem: A bond is currently priced at a premium to par. This MOST likely indicates that the bond's coupon rate is:

options.text: Greater than its market yield (yield to maturity)
Less than its market yield
Equal to its market yield
Equal to zero

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A bond trades at a premium when its coupon rate exceeds the market yield, because investors pay more for above-market coupons. Why the others are wrong: **B** a coupon below the yield produces a discount price; **C** a coupon equal to the yield prices the bond at par; **D** a zero-coupon bond always trades at a discount, never a premium.

questions.stem: All else equal, which bond will have the GREATEST interest rate price sensitivity (highest duration)?

options.text: A long-maturity, low-coupon bond
A short-maturity, high-coupon bond
A short-maturity, low-coupon bond
A long-maturity, high-coupon bond

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Duration rises with longer maturity and with lower coupons, so a long-maturity, low-coupon bond has the greatest price sensitivity to yield changes. Why the others are wrong: **B** short maturity and high coupon give the lowest duration; **C** short maturity limits sensitivity despite the low coupon; **D** a high coupon shortens duration relative to the low-coupon bond of the same maturity.

questions.stem: From a bondholder's perspective, an embedded call option on a bond is BEST described as:

options.text: A disadvantage, because the issuer can redeem the bond early when rates fall
An advantage, because the bondholder can force early redemption
Irrelevant, because it does not affect the bond's value
An advantage, because it raises the bond's price above an otherwise identical option-free bond

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A call option benefits the issuer, who can redeem and refinance when rates fall, capping the bondholder's price upside and creating reinvestment risk; thus a callable bond yields more and prices lower than an option-free bond. Why the others are wrong: **B** the bondholder controls a put, not a call; **C** the option clearly affects value via the issuer's right; **D** the call lowers, not raises, the price relative to an option-free bond.

questions.stem: A 1-year zero-coupon bond with a face value of $100 is priced at $96.15. Its yield to maturity (effective annual rate) is closest to:
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** For a 1-year zero, price = 100/(1 + y), so 1 + y = 100/96.15 = 1.0400, giving y = 4.0%. Why the others are wrong: **B** 3.85% is the discount ((100 - 96.15)/100) on face, not the yield on price; **C** 4.15% overstates the yield; **D** 5.0% would imply a price near $95.24, not $96.15.

questions.stem: Which two risks are MOST directly associated with investing in long-term fixed-coupon bonds? (Select two.)

options.text: Interest rate (price) risk from changes in market yields
Inflation (purchasing power) risk eroding the real value of fixed coupons
Unlimited liability risk for the bondholder
Dilution risk from the issuance of additional shares

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Long-term fixed-coupon bonds are exposed to interest rate risk—their prices fall when yields rise—and to inflation risk, which erodes the real purchasing power of fixed coupons. Why the others are wrong: **C** bondholders are creditors with limited exposure, not unlimited liability; **D** dilution affects equity holders, not bondholders.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes a forward contract from a futures contract?

options.text: Futures are standardized and exchange-traded with daily mark-to-market, while forwards are customized OTC contracts
Forwards are standardized and exchange-traded, while futures are customized OTC contracts
Futures have no counterparty credit risk because they are unregulated
Forwards are settled daily through a clearinghouse, while futures settle only at expiration

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Futures are standardized, traded on exchanges, and marked to market daily through a clearinghouse; forwards are private, customized over-the-counter agreements. Why the others are wrong: **B** reverses the two definitions; **C** futures reduce credit risk through the clearinghouse and margining and are regulated, not unregulated; **D** it is futures, not forwards, that settle daily via a clearinghouse.

questions.stem: At expiration, the payoff to the holder of a long European call option with strike price X on an underlying priced at ST is:

options.text: max(0, ST - X)
max(0, X - ST)
ST - X, which can be negative
X - ST, which can be negative

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A call gives the right, not the obligation, to buy at X; the holder exercises only when ST > X, so the payoff is max(0, ST - X). Why the others are wrong: **B** max(0, X - ST) is the payoff to a long put; **C** the call payoff is floored at zero and cannot be negative because exercise is optional; **D** describes an unbounded short/put-type payoff that ignores optionality.

questions.stem: Two portfolios that produce identical future cash flows trade at different prices. According to the principle of no-arbitrage (the law of one price), an investor should:

options.text: Buy the cheaper portfolio and sell the more expensive one to lock in a riskless profit
Buy both portfolios to diversify the position
Short both portfolios because identical cash flows imply both are overvalued
Do nothing, because identical cash flows guarantee identical prices in all cases

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Arbitrage exploits a violation of the law of one price: buy the underpriced replicating portfolio and sell the overpriced one, earning a riskless profit with no net investment until prices converge. Why the others are wrong: **B** buying both incurs cost without exploiting the mispricing; **C** shorting both is not riskless and ignores the relative mispricing; **D** the prices are observed to differ, which is precisely the arbitrage opportunity.

questions.stem: A private equity firm acquires a mature public company using a large amount of debt and takes it private. This strategy is BEST described as a:

options.text: Leveraged buyout (LBO)
Venture capital investment
Mezzanine equity carve-out
Greenfield infrastructure project

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A leveraged buyout uses significant borrowed funds to acquire a company, often a mature business with stable cash flows, and take it private. Why the others are wrong: **B** venture capital funds early-stage, high-growth startups, not mature public firms; **C** a carve-out spins off a subsidiary and is not defined by heavy acquisition leverage; **D** a greenfield project builds new infrastructure rather than buying an existing company.

questions.stem: A hedge fund charges a '2 and 20' fee structure. The '20' refers to:

options.text: An incentive (performance) fee equal to 20% of the fund's profits
An annual management fee of 20% of assets under management
A 20% redemption penalty charged on all withdrawals
A guaranteed 20% annual return to investors

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** In '2 and 20', the 2% is the annual management fee on assets and the 20% is the incentive fee charged on profits, often subject to a hurdle rate and high-water mark. Why the others are wrong: **B** 20% would be an implausibly large management fee—the management fee is the 2%; **C** the 20% is not a redemption penalty; **D** hedge funds do not guarantee returns.

questions.stem: Which two characteristics are commonly cited as potential benefits of adding alternative investments to a traditional stock-and-bond portfolio? (Select two.)

options.text: Potential diversification from low correlation with traditional assets
Potential for higher returns relative to traditional asset classes
Greater liquidity than publicly traded stocks and bonds
Lower management fees than index mutual funds

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Alternatives are added largely for diversification (often lower correlation with stocks and bonds) and the potential for higher returns. Why the others are wrong: **C** many alternatives (private equity, real estate, hedge funds) are less liquid than public securities, not more; **D** alternatives typically charge higher fees than index funds, not lower.

questions.stem: According to the capital asset pricing model (CAPM), a stock with a beta greater than 1.0 should have an expected return that is:

options.text: Greater than the expected return on the market portfolio
Equal to the risk-free rate
Less than the risk-free rate
Equal to the market return regardless of beta

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** CAPM gives E(R) = Rf + beta(E(Rm) - Rf). With beta > 1 and a positive market risk premium, the stock's expected return exceeds the market's (whose beta is 1). Why the others are wrong: **B** the return equals Rf only if beta = 0; **C** a return below Rf would require negative beta with a positive premium; **D** expected return varies with beta, so it does not simply equal the market return.

questions.stem: Two risky assets are combined into a portfolio. The diversification benefit (risk reduction for a given expected return) is GREATEST when the correlation between the two assets' returns is:

options.text: -1.0 (perfectly negative)
+1.0 (perfectly positive)
0.0 (uncorrelated)
+0.5 (moderately positive)

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The lower the correlation, the greater the diversification benefit; at a correlation of -1.0 the assets move exactly opposite, allowing the greatest risk reduction (in theory a riskless combination). Why the others are wrong: **B** at +1.0 there is no diversification benefit—portfolio risk is just the weighted average; **C** zero correlation gives meaningful but not maximal benefit; **D** +0.5 gives even less benefit than zero correlation.

questions.stem: In the investment policy statement (IPS), an investor's required liquidity needs and investment time horizon are BEST classified as:

options.text: Constraints
Return objectives
Risk objectives
Capital market expectations

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** An IPS separates objectives (risk and return) from constraints; liquidity needs and time horizon are classic constraints, alongside taxes, legal/regulatory factors, and unique circumstances. Why the others are wrong: **B** return objectives state the desired return, not liquidity/horizon; **C** risk objectives address ability and willingness to bear risk; **D** capital market expectations are inputs to forming the strategic asset allocation, not investor constraints.

questions.stem: Which two statements correctly describe systematic (market) risk in portfolio theory? (Select two.)

options.text: It cannot be eliminated through diversification
It is the risk for which investors are compensated with a risk premium
It can be fully diversified away by holding many securities
It is also called firm-specific or unsystematic risk

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Systematic risk is non-diversifiable market-wide risk, and because it cannot be diversified away, it is the risk for which investors earn a risk premium (the basis of CAPM). Why the others are wrong: **C** it is unsystematic (firm-specific) risk that diversification removes, not systematic risk; **D** firm-specific/unsystematic risk is the opposite of systematic risk.

questions.stem: A CFA charterholder works in a country whose securities laws are less strict than the CFA Institute Code and Standards. Under Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, which body of rules must she follow?

options.text: The Code and Standards only, ignoring all local law
The local law only, because she is physically located there
The stricter of the applicable law or the Code and Standards
Whichever rule is less restrictive so as to remain competitive

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Standard I(A) requires members to comply with the more strict of applicable law or the Code and Standards when they differ. Why the others are wrong: **B** following lax local law alone can breach the Code, which still applies; **A** members must also obey applicable law, not ignore it; **D** choosing the less restrictive rule is the opposite of the standard.

questions.stem: An adviser presents a model portfolio's hypothetical back-tested results to prospects as if they were actual returns the firm earned for clients. This MOST likely violates which standard?

options.text: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
Standard III(B) Fair Dealing
Standard IV(A) Loyalty to Employer
Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Standard I(C) prohibits misrepresentations; presenting hypothetical or back-tested results as actual realized performance is a deceptive misstatement of fact. Why the others are wrong: **B** fair dealing concerns treating clients equitably in recommendations and trades; **C** loyalty addresses duties to the employer; **D** priority of transactions governs client trades ahead of personal trades, none of which is the core issue here.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager recommends a high-risk, illiquid private placement to a retired client whose investment policy statement specifies a low risk tolerance and a need for current income. This BEST implicates which standard?

options.text: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard III(C) Suitability
Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Programs

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Standard III(C) Suitability requires that recommendations fit the client's stated objectives and constraints in the IPS; an illiquid, high-risk holding clashes with low risk tolerance and income needs. Why the others are wrong: **A** market manipulation involves distorting prices or volume; **C** diligence concerns the research basis, not the client fit; **D** Standard VII(A) governs exam conduct, which is unrelated.

questions.stem: An analyst receives a corporate-finance role on a deal in which she personally owns a meaningful equity stake in the target company. Under Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts, what must she do?

options.text: Disclose the ownership conflict fully and fairly to her employer and clients
Sell the shares secretly so no conflict needs to be reported
Disclose only if a client specifically asks about her holdings
Do nothing, because personal holdings are never a reportable conflict

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Standard VI(A) requires prominent, full, and fair disclosure of any matter that could impair independence or objectivity, including beneficial ownership in a subject company. Why the others are wrong: **B** concealing the conflict by trading does not satisfy the duty to disclose; **C** disclosure is proactive, not contingent on a client's question; **D** personal beneficial ownership is a classic reportable conflict.

questions.stem: A supervisor learns that the firm has no procedures in place to detect employee trading violations, and management refuses to adopt any. Under Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors, the supervisor should MOST appropriately:

options.text: Decline supervisory responsibility in writing until adequate compliance procedures are established
Accept the role and rely on employees to self-report any violations
Delegate all supervision so personal responsibility is eliminated
Ignore the gap because compliance systems are solely management's duty

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under Standard IV(C), a supervisor who cannot discharge supervisory duties because adequate compliance procedures are absent should decline the responsibility in writing until they are put in place. Why the others are wrong: **B** relying on self-reporting is not reasonable supervision; **C** delegation does not relieve the supervisor of responsibility; **D** supervisors share responsibility for an effective compliance system and cannot simply ignore the gap.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions, which two practices are appropriate when a member trades for personal accounts as well as client accounts? (Select two.)

options.text: Execute client and employer transactions before beneficial-ownership (personal) transactions
Ensure personal trading does not adversely affect clients' interests
Front-run client orders to secure a better personal price
Allocate the best fills to the manager's own account first

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Standard VI(B) requires that clients and the employer come first and that personal transactions never disadvantage them. Why the others are wrong: **C** front-running client orders is a direct violation of priority of transactions; **D** giving the best executions to the personal account ahead of clients also violates the standard.

questions.stem: A trader places a series of matched buy and sell orders in a thinly traded stock solely to create the appearance of active trading and lure in other investors. This conduct BEST violates which standard?

options.text: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity
Standard V(B) Communication with Clients

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Standard II(B) Market Manipulation prohibits practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume to deceive market participants, such as wash or matched trades. Why the others are wrong: **B** confidentiality concerns safeguarding client information; **C** independence addresses gifts and pressures on objectivity; **D** communication governs how recommendations are conveyed, not transaction-based deception.

questions.stem: A nominal annual rate of 8% is compounded quarterly. The effective annual rate (EAR) is closest to:
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** EAR = (1 + periodic rate)^m - 1 = (1 + 0.08/4)^4 - 1 = (1.02)^4 - 1 = 1.08243 - 1 = 8.24%. Why the others are wrong: **B** 8.00% ignores intra-year compounding (the stated nominal rate); **A** 8.16% reflects semiannual, not quarterly, compounding; **D** 2.00% is just the quarterly periodic rate, not the annual effective rate.

questions.stem: An investor buys one share for $100 at time 0. At the end of year 1 she receives a $4 dividend and buys a second share for $110. At the end of year 2 she receives $4 per share and sells both shares for $120 each. Which statement about the money-weighted and time-weighted returns is MOST accurate?

options.text: The money-weighted return reflects the timing and size of the cash flows, while the time-weighted return does not
The time-weighted return is the internal rate of return on the cash flows
The money-weighted return is unaffected by when the investor adds money
The two measures are always identical for any cash-flow pattern

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The money-weighted return is the IRR of the portfolio's cash flows and is therefore sensitive to the amount and timing of contributions and withdrawals; the time-weighted return removes those effects by compounding period returns. Why the others are wrong: **B** the IRR is the money-weighted, not time-weighted, return; **C** the money-weighted return is precisely affected by contribution timing; **D** the two differ whenever external cash flows occur.

questions.stem: In a simple linear regression of a stock's excess return on the market's excess return, the estimated slope coefficient is BEST interpreted as:

options.text: The expected change in the stock's excess return for a one-unit change in the market's excess return
The proportion of total variation in the stock explained by the market
The stock's expected return when the market's excess return is zero
The standard deviation of the regression residuals

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** In Y = b0 + b1X + e, the slope b1 measures the expected change in the dependent variable (stock excess return) per one-unit change in the independent variable (market excess return). Why the others are wrong: **B** that is the coefficient of determination (R-squared); **C** the value of Y when X is zero is the intercept b0; **D** the dispersion of residuals is the standard error of the estimate, not the slope.

questions.stem: A 10% increase in the price of a good leads to a 5% decrease in quantity demanded. The own-price elasticity of demand indicates that demand for this good is:

options.text: Perfectly elastic
Elastic, with an elasticity of about -2.0
Unit elastic, with an elasticity of -1.0
Inelastic, with an elasticity of about -0.5

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Price elasticity = %change in quantity / %change in price = -5% / 10% = -0.5; an absolute value below 1 means demand is inelastic. Why the others are wrong: **B** -2.0 would require quantity to fall 20%, the inverse of the given ratio; **C** unit elasticity needs equal percentage changes; **A** perfectly elastic demand implies an infinite response to any price change.

questions.stem: In a simple Keynesian model, the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is 0.8. The government spending multiplier is closest to:
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The simple spending multiplier = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / (1 - 0.8) = 1 / 0.2 = 5.0. Why the others are wrong: **B** 1.25 uses 1/MPC rather than 1/(1 - MPC); **C** 0.8 is the MPC itself; **D** 0.2 is the marginal propensity to save (1 - MPC), the denominator, not the multiplier.

questions.stem: The spot rate is 1.10 USD/EUR and the 1-year forward rate is 1.12 USD/EUR. With the price currency (USD) quoted per unit of the base currency (EUR), the euro is trading at a forward:

options.text: Discount, because more dollars are needed forward than spot
Premium, because the forward price of the euro exceeds its spot price
Premium, because the dollar buys more euros forward
Parity, because spot and forward rates are economically equal

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When the forward price of the base currency (EUR) is higher than its spot price (1.12 > 1.10 USD/EUR), the base currency trades at a forward premium. Why the others are wrong: **A** needing more dollars per euro forward is a premium on the euro, not a discount; **C** the dollar actually buys fewer euros forward; **D** a 2-cent gap is not parity, and a forward premium/discount typically reflects an interest rate differential.

questions.stem: A company reports net income of $10 million, preferred dividends of $1 million, and a weighted average of 3 million common shares outstanding. Its basic earnings per share (EPS) is closest to:
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Basic EPS = (net income - preferred dividends) / weighted average common shares = (10 - 1) / 3 = 9 / 3 = $3.00. Why the others are wrong: **B** $3.33 forgets to subtract the $1M preferred dividends; **C** $3.67 adds rather than subtracts the preferred dividends; **A** $0.30 inverts the calculation.

questions.stem: Using the indirect method, a company starts with net income and is computing cash flow from operations. An increase in accounts receivable during the period should be:

options.text: Subtracted, because revenue was recognized but cash has not yet been collected
Added, because higher receivables mean more cash was collected
Ignored, because receivables are a balance-sheet item only
Added to investing activities rather than operating activities

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under the indirect method, an increase in accounts receivable means sales were booked in net income without a matching cash inflow, so the increase is subtracted to convert accrual income to cash. Why the others are wrong: **B** a rise in receivables means less cash collected, not more; **C** working-capital changes must be adjusted, not ignored; **D** receivable changes belong to operating, not investing, activities.

questions.stem: Compared with the straight-line method, an accelerated depreciation method (e.g., double-declining balance) will, in the early years of an asset's life, MOST likely result in:

options.text: Identical depreciation expense in every year
Lower depreciation expense and higher reported net income
Higher depreciation expense and lower reported net income
Higher net income and higher ending asset carrying value

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Accelerated methods front-load depreciation, so early-year expense is higher and reported net income is lower than under straight-line (the carrying value also declines faster). Why the others are wrong: **B** reverses the early-year effect; **A** the two methods give different yearly expense even though total depreciation over the life is the same; **D** higher early depreciation reduces both net income and the carrying value, not raises them.

questions.stem: A deferred tax liability MOST commonly arises when:

options.text: Taxable income is currently lower than pretax financial income, so taxes are deferred to future periods
Taxable income is currently higher than pretax financial income
A company has a net operating loss carryforward
Tax rates are zero in all periods

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A deferred tax liability reflects taxes expected to be paid later, arising when taxable income is temporarily below pretax accounting income (e.g., using accelerated depreciation for tax but straight-line for reporting). Why the others are wrong: **B** taxable income above book income creates a deferred tax asset, not a liability; **C** loss carryforwards generate deferred tax assets; **D** zero tax rates would produce no deferred tax balances at all.

questions.stem: An analyst assessing earnings quality is concerned about a high level of accruals. Which two indicators would MOST suggest lower-quality (less sustainable) earnings? (Select two.)

options.text: Net income consistently and substantially exceeding operating cash flow
Revenue recognized well before the related cash is collected, with a rising receivables-to-sales ratio
Operating cash flow closely tracking net income over time
Conservative, consistently applied accounting policies

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Earnings backed largely by accruals rather than cash, shown by net income persistently above operating cash flow and by revenue booked ahead of collections (rising receivables/sales), are lower quality and less sustainable. Why the others are wrong: **C** cash flow tracking net income signals higher-quality earnings; **D** conservative, consistent policies support, rather than undermine, earnings quality.

questions.stem: The conflict of interest that can arise when a company's managers pursue their own interests at the expense of the shareholders who own the firm is BEST described as:

options.text: Adverse selection in lending
The principal-agent (agency) problem
The free-rider problem among bondholders
A negative externality

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When managers (agents) act in their own interest rather than that of shareholders (principals), the resulting conflict is the principal-agent problem, a central theme of corporate governance. Why the others are wrong: **A** adverse selection involves information asymmetry before a transaction, typically in markets; **C** the free-rider problem concerns parties benefiting without contributing, not the manager-owner conflict; **D** an externality is a spillover cost or benefit to third parties.

questions.stem: A project costs $1,000 today and is expected to generate level after-tax cash inflows of $250 per year. Its payback period is:

options.text: 4 years
2.5 years
5 years
0.25 years

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** With equal annual cash flows, payback period = initial outlay / annual cash flow = 1,000 / 250 = 4 years. Why the others are wrong: **B** 2.5 years would require $400 annual inflows; **C** 5 years implies $200 inflows; **D** 0.25 years inverts the ratio (250/1,000).

questions.stem: A company shortens the time it takes to collect receivables and extends the time it takes to pay suppliers, while inventory days are unchanged. The MOST likely effect on its cash conversion cycle (net operating cycle) is that it will:

options.text: Shorten, improving the firm's liquidity position
Lengthen, worsening the firm's liquidity position
Remain unchanged, because the two effects always offset
Become negative only if inventory days are also reduced

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Cash conversion cycle = days of inventory + days of receivables - days of payables. Collecting receivables faster lowers receivable days and paying suppliers slower raises payable days; both shorten the cycle and improve liquidity. Why the others are wrong: **B** the changes shorten, not lengthen, the cycle; **C** the two effects reinforce each other here rather than offsetting; **D** the cycle shortens regardless, and a negative cycle is not contingent on cutting inventory days.

questions.stem: A price-weighted index contains two stocks priced at $20 and $40, with a divisor of 2. If the $40 stock undergoes a 2-for-1 split (its price becomes $20) and the divisor is adjusted to keep the index unchanged, the new divisor is closest to:
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Before the split the index = (20 + 40)/2 = 30. After the split the prices sum to 20 + 20 = 40, so the divisor must satisfy 40/d = 30, giving d = 40/30 = 1.33. Why the others are wrong: **B** 2.00 is the old divisor, which would now give an index of 20, breaking continuity; **C** 1.00 would yield 40; **A** 1.50 would yield about 26.7, neither equal to 30.

questions.stem: A stock trades at $30 and has trailing earnings per share of $2.50. Its trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is:
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** P/E = price per share / earnings per share = 30 / 2.50 = 12.0. Why the others are wrong: **B** 0.083 is the earnings yield (E/P), the inverse of P/E; **C** 7.5 misdivides (e.g., 30/4); **D** 75.0 misplaces the decimal in EPS (30/0.40).

questions.stem: A non-U.S. company's shares are bundled and trade on a U.S. exchange in U.S. dollars, allowing domestic investors to gain exposure without dealing in the foreign market directly. This instrument is BEST described as a:

options.text: Closed-end mutual fund
Convertible bond
Depositary receipt (e.g., an American Depositary Receipt)
Stock warrant

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A depositary receipt, such as an ADR, is a negotiable certificate representing ownership in a foreign company's shares that trades on a U.S. exchange in U.S. dollars. Why the others are wrong: **B** a convertible bond is debt convertible into equity, not a foreign-share wrapper; **A** a closed-end fund is a pooled vehicle, not a single company's listed shares abroad; **D** a warrant is a long-dated call-like right to buy shares, not foreign-share representation.

questions.stem: According to Porter's five forces framework for industry analysis, which two of the following are among the forces that shape industry competition and profitability? (Select two.)

options.text: The threat of new entrants
The bargaining power of suppliers
The level of the risk-free interest rate
The country's marginal income tax rate

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Porter's five forces are the threat of new entrants, supplier power, buyer power, the threat of substitutes, and rivalry among existing competitors. Why the others are wrong: **C** the risk-free rate is a macro/valuation input, not one of the five competitive forces; **D** tax rates affect after-tax profits broadly but are not part of Porter's framework.

questions.stem: A bond with a 6% annual coupon and a $1,000 face value is currently priced at $960. Its current yield is closest to:
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Current yield = annual coupon / current price = $60 / $960 = 6.25%. Why the others are wrong: **A** 6.00% is the coupon rate based on face value, not on the discounted price; **C** 5.76% divides the coupon by face times a wrong factor (e.g., 60/1,041); **D** 4.00% confuses the discount from par with the yield.

questions.stem: Convexity is MOST useful in bond analysis because it captures the fact that, for a given large change in yield, the price-yield relationship is:

options.text: Curved, so duration alone understates the price gain when yields fall and overstates the price loss when yields rise
Linear, so duration alone perfectly predicts the price change
Such that price always rises when yields rise
Independent of the size of the yield change

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The price-yield curve for an option-free bond is convex; duration is a linear approximation, so adding convexity corrects it—actual prices rise more than duration predicts when yields fall and fall less when yields rise. Why the others are wrong: **B** the relationship is curved, not linear, so duration alone is imperfect for large moves; **C** prices fall, not rise, when yields rise; **D** the approximation error grows with the size of the yield change, so it is not independent of it.

questions.stem: All else equal, a widening of the credit spread on a corporate bond relative to a comparable government benchmark will MOST likely cause the corporate bond's price to:

options.text: Fall, because the higher required yield lowers the present value of its cash flows
Rise, because a wider spread signals improving credit quality
Remain unchanged, because spreads do not affect price
Rise, because the coupon automatically increases with the spread

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A wider credit spread raises the bond's required yield; since price moves inversely with yield, the bond's price falls. Why the others are wrong: **B** a widening spread signals deteriorating, not improving, credit quality; **C** spreads are part of the discount rate and clearly affect price; **D** a fixed-coupon bond's coupon does not rise with the spread—only the discount rate changes.

questions.stem: Which two statements about securitization and asset-backed securities (ABS) are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: A pool of assets is transferred to a special purpose entity (SPE) that issues securities backed by those assets
Securitization can use a senior/subordinated (tranched) structure to redistribute credit risk among investors
ABS investors always have a direct, unsecured claim on the originating company's general assets
Securitization eliminates all prepayment and default risk for investors

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Securitization transfers a pool of assets to a bankruptcy-remote SPE that issues securities, and credit risk is often carved into senior and subordinated tranches with different priorities. Why the others are wrong: **C** ABS holders have claims on the segregated asset pool in the SPE, not a general unsecured claim on the originator; **D** securitization reallocates but does not eliminate prepayment and default risk.

questions.stem: Put-call parity for European options on a non-dividend-paying stock is BEST expressed as:

options.text: Call price - Put price = present value of the strike - underlying price
Call price + underlying price = Put price + present value of the strike
Call price + present value of the strike = Put price + underlying price
Call price x Put price = underlying price x present value of the strike

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Put-call parity states c + X/(1+r)^T = p + S0, i.e., a call plus the present value of the strike (a fiduciary call) equals a put plus the underlying (a protective put). Why the others are wrong: **B** pairs the call with the underlying and the put with the PV of the strike, which is incorrect; **A** rearranges with the signs reversed; **D** the relationship is additive (a no-arbitrage equality), not multiplicative.

questions.stem: In a plain-vanilla interest rate swap, one party agrees to pay a fixed rate and receive a floating rate on a notional principal. The notional principal in such a swap is:

options.text: Used only to calculate the periodic interest payments and is generally not exchanged
Exchanged in full between the parties at initiation and again at maturity
Paid entirely to the fixed-rate payer at the start of the swap
Equal to the net present value of all expected cash flows

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** In a plain-vanilla interest rate swap, the notional principal is a reference amount used to compute the fixed and floating interest payments; it is not exchanged because both legs are in the same currency. Why the others are wrong: **B** principal exchange occurs in currency swaps, not single-currency interest rate swaps; **C** the notional is not paid to either party at inception; **D** the notional is a stated reference amount, not the NPV of the cash flows.

questions.stem: A commercial property generates net operating income (NOI) of $400,000 per year and is valued using a market capitalization rate of 8%. Using the direct capitalization approach, the estimated property value is:
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Direct capitalization value = NOI / cap rate = 400,000 / 0.08 = $5,000,000. Why the others are wrong: **B** $3,200,000 multiplies NOI by the cap rate rather than dividing; **C** $32,000 multiplies and misplaces decimals; **D** $4,000,000 uses a 10% cap rate, not the given 8%.

questions.stem: A commodity futures market is described as being in contango. This means that, all else equal, the futures price is:

options.text: Above the current spot price, which tends to produce a negative roll yield for a long futures position
Below the current spot price, producing a positive roll yield for a long position
Equal to the spot price, so roll yield is always zero
Above the spot price, which guarantees a profit for long investors

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Contango is a futures curve in which futures prices exceed the spot price; a long roller sells lower-priced expiring contracts and buys higher-priced later ones, generating a negative roll yield. Why the others are wrong: **B** describes backwardation, the opposite; **C** equal spot and futures prices is neither contango nor backwardation; **D** contango does not guarantee a profit—indeed it typically drags on long returns.

questions.stem: Mezzanine financing within private capital is BEST characterized as:

options.text: Subordinated debt that often includes equity-like features such as warrants, ranking between senior debt and equity
The most senior, lowest-risk tranche of a company's capital structure
Publicly traded common equity issued in an IPO
A government grant that need not be repaid

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Mezzanine financing is subordinated (junior) debt that sits between senior debt and equity in priority and frequently carries equity kickers such as warrants to compensate for its higher risk. Why the others are wrong: **B** the most senior, lowest-risk layer is senior debt, not mezzanine; **C** mezzanine is private, hybrid debt, not public IPO equity; **D** it is repayable financing, not a non-repayable grant.

questions.stem: A portfolio has an expected return of 11%, a standard deviation of 20%, and the risk-free rate is 3%. Its Sharpe ratio is closest to:
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Sharpe ratio = (portfolio return - risk-free rate) / standard deviation = (11% - 3%) / 20% = 8 / 20 = 0.40. Why the others are wrong: **A** 0.55 forgets to subtract the risk-free rate (11/20); **C** 0.15 uses the wrong numerator (e.g., 3/20); **D** 2.50 inverts the ratio (20/8).

questions.stem: On a graph of expected return against standard deviation, the line that runs from the risk-free rate through the market portfolio and represents the best risk-return combinations available to all investors is the:

options.text: Capital market line (CML)
Security market line (SML)
Characteristic line
Indifference curve

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The capital market line plots expected return against total risk (standard deviation) and runs from the risk-free asset tangent to the efficient frontier at the market portfolio, defining the best feasible portfolios. Why the others are wrong: **B** the SML plots expected return against beta (systematic risk), not total risk; **C** the characteristic line regresses an asset's returns on the market's; **D** an indifference curve reflects an investor's risk preferences, not the market opportunity set.

questions.stem: In mean-variance portfolio theory, a more risk-averse investor's indifference curves are BEST described as:

options.text: Steeper, requiring more additional expected return to accept each additional unit of risk
Flatter, requiring less additional return to accept more risk
Downward sloping, because more risk is always preferred
Horizontal, because risk does not affect utility

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A more risk-averse investor demands greater compensation for taking on risk, so their indifference curves are steeper in expected return-standard deviation space. Why the others are wrong: **B** flatter curves indicate lower, not higher, risk aversion; **C** risk-averse investors dislike risk, so curves slope upward (more risk requires more return), and more risk is not preferred; **D** horizontal curves would mean risk is irrelevant to utility, contradicting risk aversion.

questions.stem: An introduction to risk management and fintech covers tools used in modern investment management. Which two are commonly cited applications of fintech in this context? (Select two.)

options.text: Using big data and machine learning to analyze large, unstructured datasets for investment insights
Robo-advisory platforms that deliver automated, algorithm-based portfolio advice
Eliminating the need for any risk governance framework
Guaranteeing positive returns by removing market risk entirely

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Fintech applications include analyzing big data with machine learning to extract investment insights and robo-advisers that automate portfolio construction and advice. Why the others are wrong: **C** fintech supports, but does not eliminate the need for, a sound risk governance framework; **D** no technology can remove market risk or guarantee positive returns.

questions.stem: An investor wants to buy a stock currently trading at $50 but is only willing to pay $48 or less. The MOST appropriate order to achieve this is a:

options.text: Market-on-close buy order
Market buy order
Stop-loss sell order at $48
Limit buy order at $48

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A limit buy order sets the maximum price the investor will pay, so a $48 limit executes only at $48 or lower, satisfying the price constraint. Why the others are wrong: **B** a market order fills at the prevailing price (about $50), ignoring the limit; **C** a stop-loss sell is a sell trigger for an existing long position, not a way to buy below market; **A** a market-on-close order still fills at the (unconstrained) closing price.

questions.stem: A 91-day U.S. Treasury bill with a face value of $100 is quoted at a bank discount yield of 4%. Its purchase price is closest to:
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The bank discount yield is quoted on face value using a 360-day year: dollar discount = 0.04 x (91/360) x 100 = $1.011, so price = 100 - 1.011 = $98.99. Why the others are wrong: **B** $96.00 applies the 4% to the full year rather than 91/360; **C** $99.60 uses 90/360 of 1% or otherwise miscomputes the day fraction; **D** $100.40 adds the discount instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: An analyst discovers that a colleague has been falsifying client account statements. The analyst reports the misconduct to regulators in good faith. Under Standard I(D) Misconduct and the broader Code, this whistleblowing is BEST viewed as:

options.text: Consistent with the Code, because acting to protect the integrity of the market and clients takes priority over loyalty to a colleague or employer
A violation of Standard IV(A) Loyalty, because the analyst harmed the employer's reputation
Permissible only if the analyst first obtained written permission from the colleague
Required to be kept confidential under Standard III(E) and therefore prohibited

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Reporting illegal or unethical activity that harms clients or markets is consistent with the Code; the duty to protect market integrity and clients outweighs loyalty to an employer when they conflict. Why the others are wrong: **B** loyalty does not require concealing fraud—whistleblowing in these circumstances does not violate Standard IV(A); **C** no permission from the wrongdoer is needed; **D** confidentiality under III(E) protects legitimate client information, not the cover-up of illegal acts.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(C) Record Retention, when a member changes firms, the supporting research records that document investment recommendations:

options.text: May always be copied and taken because the member personally created them
Generally belong to the firm and cannot be taken to the new employer without permission
Must be destroyed immediately upon resignation
Need not be retained at all, since the Code sets no retention expectation

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Records supporting research and recommendations are normally the property of the firm; a departing member must re-create the supporting documentation at the new firm rather than take the originals without consent. Why the others are wrong: **A** the member's authorship does not transfer ownership of firm records; **C** the firm must retain records (commonly seven years is recommended), not destroy them; **D** the standard expects members and firms to maintain records that support their analysis.

questions.stem: An analyst uses the mosaic theory to reach a conclusion. The mosaic theory holds that an analyst may:

options.text: Trade freely on material nonpublic information so long as several sources are combined
Disregard public information entirely and rely only on insider tips
Combine public information with non-material nonpublic information to form a conclusion and act on it, without violating Standard II(A)
Share material nonpublic information with clients if it is mixed with public data

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The mosaic theory lets an analyst assemble public information together with non-material nonpublic pieces into a conclusion that may itself be material; reaching and acting on such a conclusion does not breach Standard II(A). Why the others are wrong: **A** combining sources never legitimizes trading on genuinely material nonpublic information; **B** the theory relies on public data, not on insider tips alone; **D** disseminating material nonpublic information remains prohibited regardless of any public mix.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager directs the firm's trades to a particular broker that charges higher commissions but, in return, gives the manager personal travel perks unrelated to client research. This MOST directly violates the duty of:

options.text: Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
Loyalty, prudence, and care owed to clients under Standard III(A)
Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care requires managers to act for the client's benefit; client brokerage must purchase goods or services that benefit clients, not personal perks, and seeking best execution is part of that duty. Why the others are wrong: **A** Reference to CFA Institute concerns use of the marks; **B** the issue is misuse of soft dollars, not insider information; **D** no specific legal-knowledge breach is the core of this conduct.

questions.stem: A candidate in the CFA Program posts in an online forum that the upcoming exam will likely emphasize derivatives, based on her personal study impressions. A second candidate posts actual questions he recalls from the exam he just sat. Under Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs:

options.text: Both candidates violate the standard equally
The second candidate violates the standard by disclosing confidential exam content, while the first candidate's general study opinion does not
Neither candidate violates the standard, because forum posts are private
Only the first candidate violates the standard, for expressing an exam opinion

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Standard VII(A) prohibits disclosing confidential exam information; recalling and sharing actual questions breaches it, whereas voicing a general personal opinion about emphasis does not reveal confidential content. Why the others are wrong: **A** the two acts are not equivalent—only one discloses confidential material; **C** posts are not private and the prohibition still applies; **D** expressing a study opinion is permitted, so the first candidate does not violate the standard.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, which two circumstances permit a member to disclose otherwise confidential client information? (Select two.)

options.text: When disclosure is required by law
When the client permits the disclosure
When disclosing it would help win a new prospective client
When a colleague at a competitor firm simply asks for it

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Confidential client information may be disclosed when the law requires it or when the client consents (it may also be shared with the member's compliance function regarding illegal activities). Why the others are wrong: **C** using confidential information to attract new business is an impermissible breach of the duty; **D** a competitor's request gives no right to reveal a client's confidential information.

questions.stem: Place the steps of a structured ethical decision-making framework in their typical order.

options.text: Identify the relevant facts, stakeholders, and ethical principles at stake
Consider alternative actions and seek additional guidance (e.g., from compliance or the Code)
Decide on a course of action and act
Reflect on the outcome and assess whether the decision was sound

questions.explanation: The correct order is A, B, C, D. A sound ethical decision-making framework begins by identifying the situation: the relevant facts, the affected stakeholders, and the ethical principles and duties at stake. It then moves to considering alternative actions and seeking additional guidance, such as input from compliance, a trusted mentor, or the Code and Standards, so the decision is not made in isolation. Only after weighing alternatives does the member decide on and carry out a course of action. Finally, the member reflects on the outcome, evaluating whether the decision achieved an ethical result and what could be improved next time. Gathering facts must precede evaluating options, action follows deliberation, and reflection logically comes last.

questions.stem: An investment will pay $500 at the end of each year for 4 years. If the appropriate discount rate is 10%, the present value of this ordinary annuity is closest to:
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** PV of an ordinary annuity = PMT x [1 - (1 + r)^-n]/r = 500 x [1 - 1.10^-4]/0.10 = 500 x 3.16987 = $1,584.93. Why the others are wrong: **A** $2,000 is the undiscounted sum of the payments; **B** $1,743.42 is the present value of an annuity due (payments at the start of each period); **D** $1,442.66 discounts too aggressively (e.g., uses one extra period).

questions.stem: Monthly returns on a fund have a mean of 1.0% and a standard deviation of 4.0%. Assuming returns are approximately normally distributed, roughly what percentage of months would be expected to fall between -7.0% and +9.0% (i.e., within two standard deviations of the mean)?

options.text: About 68%
About 95%
About 99.7%
About 50%

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The interval -7% to +9% spans the mean (1%) plus and minus two standard deviations (2 x 4% = 8%). For a normal distribution, about 95% of observations lie within +/-2 standard deviations. Why the others are wrong: **A** 68% corresponds to +/-1 standard deviation; **C** 99.7% corresponds to +/-3 standard deviations; **D** 50% reflects only one side of the mean, not a two-sided 2-sigma band.

questions.stem: The central limit theorem states that, for a population with finite variance, the sampling distribution of the sample mean:

options.text: Is normal only if the underlying population is itself normal
Has a standard deviation that increases with the square root of the sample size
Becomes increasingly skewed as the sample size grows
Approaches a normal distribution as the sample size becomes large, regardless of the population's distribution

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The central limit theorem says the distribution of the sample mean approaches normal as sample size grows (commonly n >= 30), whatever the shape of the population, provided variance is finite. Why the others are wrong: **A** normality of the mean does not require a normal population—that is the theorem's power; **B** the standard error equals sigma/sqrt(n), which decreases, not increases, with n; **C** the sampling distribution becomes more, not less, normal as n grows.

questions.stem: A market is dominated by a few large firms whose pricing decisions are interdependent, so each firm must anticipate rivals' reactions. This market structure is BEST described as:

options.text: Perfect competition
Oligopoly
Monopolistic competition
Pure monopoly

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An oligopoly has a small number of large, interdependent sellers, so strategic behavior and reaction to rivals (often analyzed with game theory) is central. Why the others are wrong: **A** perfect competition has many price-taking firms with no interdependence; **C** monopolistic competition has many firms selling differentiated products with little mutual dependence; **D** a pure monopoly has a single seller with no rivals to anticipate.

questions.stem: Nominal GDP grew 6% over a year while the GDP deflator rose 4%. Real GDP growth over the period is closest to:
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Real GDP growth approximately equals nominal GDP growth minus inflation (the change in the GDP deflator): 6% - 4% = 2%. Why the others are wrong: **A** 10% adds inflation to nominal growth instead of subtracting it; **B** 6% is nominal growth, which has not been adjusted for rising prices; **D** 24% multiplies the two figures, which is not how the relationship works.

questions.stem: Under the theory of purchasing power parity (PPP) and interest rate parity, which two relationships are predicted for a country with relatively high inflation and high nominal interest rates? (Select two.)

options.text: Relative PPP predicts the high-inflation country's currency will tend to depreciate over time
Covered interest rate parity implies the high-interest-rate currency will trade at a forward discount
Relative PPP predicts the high-inflation currency will steadily appreciate
Covered interest rate parity implies the high-interest-rate currency must trade at a forward premium

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Relative PPP predicts that the currency of the higher-inflation country depreciates to offset the price-level differential, and covered interest rate parity requires the higher-yielding currency to trade at a forward discount so arbitrage profits are eliminated. Why the others are wrong: **C** higher inflation implies depreciation, not appreciation; **D** the higher-interest-rate currency trades at a forward discount, not a premium.

questions.stem: Under IFRS, a company classifies dividends paid in the statement of cash flows. Which treatment is permitted that differs from US GAAP?
